If the dependency graph is a DAG with distinct roots, failures are truly independent; if there are shared ancestral dependencies (cycles in the transitive closure), failures are conditionally dependent on the shared ancestor.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the decentralized network shares a common root dependency that is not obvious (e.g., all operators use the same underlying Tier 1 ISP).","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the large service actually uses multiple distinct cloud providers and corporate entities for its internal redundancy, severing the shared root.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Dependency Graph Separability: A decentralized network, if properly architected, has a dependency graph with multiple distinct roots (e.g., different cloud providers, different DNS). A large service, even with internal redundancy, often shares a single root (e.g., a single corporate AWS account, a single root DNS). Failures appear uncorrelated under normal conditions because the shared root is not stressed. Under a failure of the shared root, the conditional probability of failure approaches 1.0, revealing the hidden correlation. Evidence distinguishing the two would be a mapping of the operational dependency graph showing whether roots are shared.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
